title: Three central banks put a boundary around the next step for cross-border FX settlement
bank: Bank of England · Monetary Authority of Singapore · Bank of Thailand
summary: The joint announcement from London, Singapore and Bangkok is notable for what the participants were prepared to take forward together. All three central banks reported that coordinated settlement could work across wholesale systems with different technologies. They identified wider participation, additional currencies and more demanding transaction scenarios as possibilities for further work. Only the Bank of England identified a dated domestic milestone: it plans a live synchronisation interface in 2028. A reader assessing a payments investment should keep that UK interface separate from any decision to run a three-country service. The announcement gives no common launch date, price or participation commitment.

The shared problem is the interval between paying one currency and receiving another. The collaboration tested whether a synchronisation operator could coordinate those payments across three central bank test environments. It included both conventional real-time gross settlement and systems using distributed ledger technology. Partior developed, connected and tested the prototype as the delivery partner. The design let participating authorities retain different domestic infrastructures. For a bank or its technology supplier, this makes interoperability a question of what a system can authorise and confirm, rather than an obligation to replace all domestic ledgers with a single platform.

The news also identifies two different potential benefits. For a bilateral trade, payment versus payment binds the completion of one currency leg to the other, addressing the risk of delivering the full principal without receiving payment. For several trades, netting offsets what participating banks owe and are owed before settlement, potentially reducing the liquidity they must assemble. The first benefit does not quantify the second. The announcement includes no sample of commercial flows, distribution of liquidity needs across settlement banks or evidence that a participant obtained lower funding costs. Its supporting volumes document experiments in central bank test environments.

The three named officials describe the result from their respective institutions’ perspectives. The Bank of England’s Tom Mutton emphasises reducing risk and improving efficiency enough to justify continued collaboration. The Monetary Authority of Singapore’s Kenneth Gay stresses that institutions increasingly settle across systems with different operating models, and that the trial demonstrates a way to connect them. The Bank of Thailand’s Pucktada Treeratpituk highlights trust in central bank money and the practical combination of technical, operating and regulatory considerations. These comments support further development without committing any of the institutions to a particular operator, a procurement award or a new legal regime. The Reserve Bank of Australia and Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas contributed policy perspectives as observers. They did not supply two additional settlement environments.

The accompanying publications divide the next questions among an executive overview, a technical report and a policy report. The authorities say future work could extend to more industry participants and jurisdictions and examine the legal arrangements needed in practice. For a prospective participant, that leaves consequential decisions outstanding: which currencies and hours would be covered, what connections a member would need, who provides liquidity during a delay and when payment is final under each domestic rulebook. The joint release establishes a basis for asking those questions across three jurisdictions. It provides no data on the effect of publication on FX prices or on the use of established settlement services.

questions.question: Which future announcement would move the project from collaboration to a service a bank can budget for?
questions.detail: Follow each operator’s published access rules, implementation timetable and participant testing material. Separate a UK interface becoming available from agreements to connect overseas systems to it. A named operator, participation criteria and reciprocal operating commitments would tell a bank more about likely revenue and integration costs than another successful laboratory demonstration.

questions.question: Which users would change how they settle if additional currency pairs were offered?
questions.detail: Compare the proposed coverage with existing payment-versus-payment eligibility and banks’ actual settlement practices. Ask correspondent banks and smaller dealers which obstacles are due to membership costs, operating hours, liquidity or trade size. This identifies whether new connections could reduce outstanding principal exposure or mostly redistribute already protected volume between competing services.

questions.question: Who would pay for the resilience and legal work needed between jurisdictions?
questions.detail: Consult prospective scheme rules, domestic legal assessments and proposed fee schedules. Identify who must provide funds, maintain connections, resolve disputed status and compensate participants for interruptions. The announcement records policy cooperation and the observer roles, but assigns none of those costs. Their distribution could determine which institutions join even if the technical service works for all three.
